notes.meaning: Paul warns Timothy that hard and dangerous times are coming. Many older writers take "the last days" to mean the whole time since Christ came, though some think especially of the time before he returns. The danger comes less from enemies outside the church than from bad people inside it. Paul says this so Timothy will not be shocked, but will be ready and watchful.

Paul lists what people will be like, and he means even people in the church. It starts with loving yourself and loving money, which Wesley calls the first roots of evil. From there come pride, harsh words, disobeying parents, ingratitude, broken promises, slander, lack of self-control, cruelty and betrayal. At the end, people love pleasure more than they love God, and love of pleasure crowds out love for God.

These people keep the outward look of religion. They carry the Christian name and go through its forms. But they reject the real power of faith, which changes the heart and makes a person holy. Paul tells Timothy to keep away from such people and not treat their religion as real.

False teachers like these slip quietly into homes instead of teaching in the open. They target people who are easy to sway, especially those weighed down by guilt. They promise relief to a troubled conscience. Such followers are always chasing some new idea, but they never come to know the truth about Jesus.

Jannes and Jambres were the names Jewish tradition gave to the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7). They tried to copy Moses' miracles so people would not believe God had sent him. The false teachers fight the truth in the same way. Their minds are twisted, and they fail the test of true faith.

These false teachers will not get far. Their foolishness will become plain to everyone, just as the magicians were shown up when they could no longer copy Moses. Error may be let loose for a while, but God keeps it on a chain. In the end, he takes off every mask.

Paul now turns to Timothy and points to his own example. Timothy knew Paul's teaching, and he knew Paul lived what he taught. He also knew Paul's goals, faith, patience and love. Paul names his sufferings in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, near Timothy's hometown, where Paul was even stoned. The Lord rescued him from them all, and that should encourage Timothy not to fear.

Paul's hard times were not unusual. Everyone who truly sets out to live a godly life in Christ will face some kind of persecution, which means being mistreated for your faith. It may be mockery, being left out, or worse. Wesley and Barnes add a warning: we should make sure we suffer for living like Christ, and not for being odd or rude.

Good people grow better by God's grace, but evil people and fakes slide from bad to worse. The way of sin runs downhill. Those who fool others end up fooling themselves too. The more they deceive, the harder it is for them to escape their own errors.

Whatever others do, Timothy must stay with what he has learned and come to trust. He can be sure of it because he knows who taught him. That was Paul, along with his godly mother Eunice and grandmother Lois. Holding on is needed, because no one is beyond the reach of temptation.

Timothy had known the Scriptures since he was a baby. At that time this meant the Old Testament, taught by his mother. These writings can make a person wise about how to be saved, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. The writers say this shows how good it is to teach children the Bible early.

"God-breathed" means Scripture comes from God himself, so it is his word and can be trusted. Because it comes from God, it is useful. It teaches what is true, shows us where we are wrong, sets us right again, and trains us to live rightly. Wesley adds that the same Spirit who inspired the writers helps those who read it with earnest prayer.

The goal is that the "man of God" is complete and fully ready for every good work. That means a minister, but also any Christian given to God. The Bible has what we need for every duty and every situation. The older writers say nothing needs to be added to it to make us complete.
